subject: math
title: Equal Groups and Fair Shares: Halves and Fourths
seo_title: Grade 1 Equal Groups and Fair Shares Worksheets: Halves and Fourths (Free, Answer Key, Ontario)
standard_text: Represent and solve equal-group problems where the total number of items is no more than 10, including problems in which each group is a half, using tools and drawings
meta_desc: Free Grade 1 math worksheets on equal groups and fair shares for the Ontario curriculum: spot equal groups, find how many in all, share between 2 and 4 friends with leftovers, halves and fourths, and why more sharers means smaller pieces. 100 picture questions with an answer key.
key_big: Equal groups have the same number in each group. Fair shares are the same size, and everything is shared.
key_sub: 5 cookies for 2 children: 2 each, then cut the last cookie into halves, so each gets 2 and a half. Two fourths are the same as one half. More sharers means smaller pieces, so a half is bigger than a fourth.
body_html:
Equal groups

Equal groups have the same number in each group. Count one group. Then check every group.

Example

There are 3 plates. Each plate has 2 cookies. How many cookies in all?

Add one 2 for each plate: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

Answer: 6 cookies

Fair shares with leftovers

A fair share means every person gets the same amount, and everything is shared. Give out the whole things first. Then cut what is left.

ChildrenLeft overCut it into
21halves
41fourths
42halves (one each)

Halves and fourths

2 equal pieces are halves. 4 equal pieces are fourths. The pieces must be the same size.

More sharers, smaller pieces

Share the same thing with more people, and each piece gets smaller. A half is bigger than a fourth.

Example

Liam shares a pizza with 1 friend. Maya shares the same size pizza with 3 friends. Who gets more?

Liam’s pizza is cut into halves. Maya’s is cut into fourths. A half is bigger.

Answer: Liam

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Calling a big piece and a small piece halvesHalves must be the same size
Thinking a fourth is bigger than a half because 4 is more than 2More pieces means smaller pieces
Counting the groups, not the things: 2 groups of 4 = 2Count all the things: 4 + 4 = 8
Leaving the leftover out, or giving it to one childCut the leftover so everyone gets the same

faq.q: What do Grade 1 students learn about fractions in Ontario?
faq.a: Grade 1 students share things fairly between 2 and 4 people and name the pieces as halves and fourths. They also learn that two fourths are the same as one half, and that a half is bigger than a fourth.

faq.q: What is a fair share in Grade 1 math?
faq.a: A fair share means every person gets the same amount and nothing is left out. If 1 cookie is left for 2 children, it is cut into halves so each child gets a half.

faq.q: Why does my child think a fourth is bigger than a half?
faq.a: Many children think 4 is more than 2, so a fourth must be bigger. Cut two same-size pieces of toast, one into halves and one into fourths, and compare the pieces.

faq.q: How can I practise equal groups and fair shares at home?
faq.a: Share snacks like crackers or grapes fairly between family members, then ask what to do with the leftover. Make equal groups of mitts, socks or toys and count how many in all.

items.q: Make the 2 plates equal. How many grapes must move?
items.e: 5 and 3 make 8. Equal is 4 and 4. Move 1 grape from the 5 to the 3. (Moving 2 gives 3 and 5. That is still not equal.)
4 and 2 make 6. Equal is 3 and 3. Move 1 strawberry from the 4 to the 2. (Moving 2 gives 2 and 4. That is still not equal.)

items.q: Make the 2 plates equal. How many apples must move?
items.e: 6 and 2 make 8. Equal is 4 and 4. Move 2 apples from the 6 to the 2. (Moving 4 gives 2 and 6. That is still not equal.)

items.q: Make the 2 plates equal. How many counters must move?
items.e: 7 and 3 make 10. Equal is 5 and 5. Move 2 counters from the 7 to the 3. (Moving 4 gives 3 and 7. That is still not equal.)

items.q: Owen and Benjamin share 8 crackers. Owen gets 5. Benjamin gets 3. Is it fair?
items.e: 5 and 3 are not the same. Owen has more. It is not fair. Fair is 4 each.

items.q: How many apples are there in all?
items.e: There are 2 groups of 4. Add: 4 + 4 = 8. (2 is the number of groups.)
There are 3 groups of 2. Add: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. (3 is the number of groups.)

items.q: How many counters are there in all?

items.q: How many cookies are there in all?

items.q: How many grapes are there in all?
items.e: There are 3 groups of 3. Add: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. (3 is the number of groups.)

items.q: How many crackers are there in all?

items.e: Each plate has 3. There are 3 plates. 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. (Not 3: that is just the plates.)

items.q: Each plate has 4 crackers. How many crackers in all?

items.q: Each plate has 2 grapes. How many grapes in all?

items.q: Put the 8 counters in 2 equal groups. How many in each group?
items.e: Give one to each group, again and again, until none are left. Each group gets 4. Check: 4 + 4 = 8.
Give one to each group, again and again, until none are left. Each group gets 5. Check: 5 + 5 = 10.

items.q: 4 children each get half an orange. How many whole oranges is that?
items.e: 2 halves make 1 whole orange. Make pairs of halves: there are 2. So that is 2 oranges.

items.q: 6 children each get half a sandwich. How many whole sandwiches is that?
items.e: 2 halves make 1 whole sandwich. Make pairs of halves: there are 3. So that is 3 sandwiches.

items.q: 10 children each get half a muffin. How many whole muffins is that?
items.e: 2 halves make 1 whole muffin. Make pairs of halves: there are 5. So that is 5 muffins.

items.q: 8 children each get half a pancake. How many whole pancakes is that?
items.e: 2 halves make 1 whole pancake. Make pairs of halves: there are 4. So that is 4 pancakes.

items.q: 2 children share 5 cookies. Each gets the same number of whole cookies. How many are left over?
items.e: Give out whole cookies, one to each child, again and again. Each child gets 2. That uses 4. 5 − 4 = 1 left over.

items.q: 2 children share 7 granola bars. Each gets the same number of whole granola bars. How many are left over?
items.e: Give out whole granola bars, one to each child, again and again. Each child gets 3. That uses 6. 7 − 6 = 1 left over.

items.q: 4 children share 6 pancakes. Each gets the same number of whole pancakes. How many are left over?
items.e: Give out whole pancakes, one to each child, again and again. Each child gets 1. That uses 4. 6 − 4 = 2 left over.

items.q: 4 children share 9 muffins. Each gets the same number of whole muffins. How many are left over?
items.e: Give out whole muffins, one to each child, again and again. Each child gets 2. That uses 8. 9 − 8 = 1 left over.

items.q: Share 9 cookies between 2 children. How many whole cookies does each child get?
items.e: Give one to each child, again and again. Each child gets 4 whole cookies, and 1 is left over. (5 each would need 10 cookies.)

items.q: Share 7 sandwiches between 2 children. How many whole sandwiches does each child get?
items.e: Give one to each child, again and again. Each child gets 3 whole sandwiches, and 1 is left over. (4 each would need 8 sandwiches.)

items.q: Share 10 granola bars between 4 children. How many whole granola bars does each child get?
items.e: Give one to each child, again and again. Each child gets 2 whole granola bars, and 2 are left over. (3 each would need 12 granola bars.)

items.q: Share 5 oranges between 4 children. How many whole oranges does each child get?
items.e: Give one to each child, again and again. Each child gets 1 whole orange, and 1 is left over. (2 each would need 8 oranges.)

items.q: 2 children share 5 pancakes fairly. How much does each child get?
items.e: Each child gets 2 whole. 1 is left over. Cut it into halves. Each child gets a half. So each gets 2 and a half pancakes.

items.q: 2 children share 7 cookies fairly. How much does each child get?
items.e: Each child gets 3 whole. 1 is left over. Cut it into halves. Each child gets a half. So each gets 3 and a half cookies.

items.q: 2 children share 3 granola bars fairly. How much does each child get?
items.e: Each child gets 1 whole. 1 is left over. Cut it into halves. Each child gets a half. So each gets 1 and a half granola bars.

items.q: 4 children share 6 sandwiches fairly. How much does each child get?
items.e: Each child gets 1 whole. 2 are left over. Cut each one into halves. That makes 4 halves, one for each child. So each gets 1 and a half sandwiches.

items.q: 4 children share 10 muffins fairly. How much does each child get?
items.e: Each child gets 2 whole. 2 are left over. Cut each one into halves. That makes 4 halves, one for each child. So each gets 2 and a half muffins.

items.q: 4 children share 5 cookies fairly. How much does each child get?
items.e: Each child gets 1 whole. 1 is left over. 4 children need 4 pieces, so cut it into fourths. Each gets a fourth. So each gets 1 and a fourth cookies.

items.q: 4 children share 9 pancakes fairly. How much does each child get?
items.e: Each child gets 2 whole. 1 is left over. 4 children need 4 pieces, so cut it into fourths. Each gets a fourth. So each gets 2 and a fourth pancakes.

items.q: 5 cookies for 2 children. Each child has 2. 1 is left over. What is fair?
items.e: 2 children need 2 equal pieces. Cut the last cookie into halves. Each child gets a half. All the cookies are shared.

items.q: 5 granola bars for 4 children. Each child has 1. 1 is left over. What is fair?
items.e: 4 children need 4 equal pieces. Cut the last granola bar into fourths. Halves make only 2 pieces.

items.q: 6 pancakes for 4 children. Each child has 1. 2 are left over. What is fair?
items.e: 2 are left and 4 children wait. Cut each one in half. That makes 4 halves: one for each child.

items.q: Noah shares 5 cookies with 1 friend like this. Is it fair?
items.e: Each plate has 2 cookies and a half. Both are the same, and all 5 cookies are shared. It is fair.

items.q: Amira shares 5 muffins with 3 friends like this. Is it fair?
items.e: One plate has 2 muffins. The others have 1. One has more, so it is not fair. Fair is to cut the last muffin into fourths: 1 and a fourth each.

items.q: Is this circle cut into halves?
items.e: There are 2 equal pieces. 2 equal pieces are halves.

items.q: Is this rectangle cut into halves?
items.e: There are 2 pieces, but they are not the same size. Halves must be equal.

items.q: Is this square cut into halves?
items.e: There are 2 equal pieces. 2 equal pieces are halves.

items.q: Is this rectangle cut into fourths?
items.e: There are 4 equal pieces. 4 equal pieces are fourths.

items.q: Is this rectangle cut into fourths?
items.e: There are 4 pieces, but they are not the same size. Fourths must be equal.

items.q: Which shape shows halves?
items.e: Shape C has 2 pieces that are the same size. That is halves.

items.q: Which shape shows halves?
items.e: Shape C has 2 pieces that are the same size. That is halves.

items.q: Which shape shows fourths?
items.e: Shape A has 4 pieces that are the same size. That is fourths.

items.q: Which shape shows fourths?
items.e: Shape B has 4 pieces that are the same size. That is fourths.

items.q: What part of the rectangle is shaded?
items.e: The rectangle has 2 equal pieces. 1 is shaded. So one half is shaded.

items.q: What part of the circle is shaded?
items.e: The circle has 4 equal pieces. 1 is shaded. So one fourth is shaded.

items.q: What part of the square is shaded?
items.e: The square has 4 equal pieces. 2 are shaded. So two fourths is shaded. Two fourths is the same as one half.

items.q: What part of the square is shaded?
items.e: The square has 4 equal pieces. 1 is shaded. So one fourth is shaded.

items.q: A shows one half. B shows two fourths. Which is more?
items.e: Both circles are the same size. The shaded parts cover the same space. Two fourths is the same as one half.

items.q: How many fourths make one half?
items.e: The shaded part is one half of the rectangle. It is 2 fourths.

items.q: Cut each half of this square into 2 equal pieces. What is the shaded part now?
items.e: Cut each half of the square in 2 and the square has 4 equal pieces. The shaded half becomes two fourths.

items.q: Which shape has one half shaded?
items.e: Shape C has 4 equal pieces and 2 are shaded: two fourths. Two fourths is the same as one half. One fourth is too little. Three fourths is too much.

items.q: Which shape has one half shaded?
items.e: Shape D has 4 equal pieces and 2 are shaded: two fourths. Two fourths is the same as one half. A small piece of 2 pieces is not a half.

items.q: How many fourths make the whole circle?
items.e: The circle has 4 equal pieces. All are shaded. 4 fourths make the whole.

items.q: How many halves make the whole rectangle?
items.e: The rectangle has 2 equal pieces. Both are shaded. 2 halves make the whole.

items.q: A and B are the same size. Which shaded piece is bigger?
items.e: A is cut into halves: 2 pieces. B is cut into fourths: 4 pieces. More pieces means smaller pieces. So A is bigger.

items.q: A and B are the same size. Which shaded piece is bigger?
items.e: A is cut into fourths. B is cut into halves. A half is bigger than a fourth, so B is bigger.

items.q: A and B are the same size. Which shaded piece is bigger?
items.e: Both squares are cut into fourths. A triangle fourth and a square fourth of the same square are the same size.

items.q: Lucas shares a pizza with 1 friend. Mateo shares the same size pizza with 3 friends. Who gets a bigger piece?
items.e: Lucas’s pizza is cut into 2 pieces: halves. Mateo’s is cut into 4 pieces: fourths. Fewer sharers means bigger pieces. Lucas gets more.

items.q: It is a snow day! Aiden cuts a pancake into halves. Kai cuts the same size pancake into fourths. Whose pieces are bigger?
items.e: Halves are 2 pieces. Fourths are 4 pieces. More pieces means smaller pieces. Aiden’s pieces are bigger.

items.q: At recess, Emma shares a granola bar fairly with 1 friend. What does each get?
items.e: Emma and 1 friend are 2 children. 2 equal pieces are halves. Each gets a half.

items.q: At lunch, Nathan shares a sandwich fairly with 3 friends. What does each get?
items.e: Nathan and 3 friends are 4 children. 4 equal pieces are fourths. Each gets a fourth. Do not forget to count Nathan.

items.q: On Thanksgiving, Sofia eats two fourths of a pumpkin pie. Hana eats one half of the same size pie. Who eats more?
items.e: Two fourths is the same as one half. They eat the same amount.

items.q: More people share the same cake. What happens to each piece?
items.e: The cake does not change. More people means more pieces, so each piece is smaller.

items.q: Leah says, “A fourth is bigger than a half, because 4 is more than 2.” Is she right?
items.e: 4 pieces are smaller than 2 pieces of the same thing. A half is bigger than a fourth.

items.q: Maya cuts her toast like this. Did she cut it in half?
items.e: Halves must be the same size. One piece is big and one is small, so they are not halves.

items.q: Zoe shares 3 granola bars fairly with 1 friend. How much does each get?
items.e: Each gets 1 whole bar. 1 is left over. Cut it into halves. Each gets 1 and a half bars.

items.q: At the cottage, 4 friends share 2 oranges fairly. How much does each get?
items.e: There are fewer oranges than friends. Cut each orange into halves. That makes 4 halves. Each friend gets a half.

items.q: At the skating rink, 4 friends share 6 cookies fairly. How much does each get?
items.e: Each friend gets 1 whole cookie. 2 are left over. Cut each one into halves. That makes 4 halves, one for each friend. Each gets 1 and a half cookies.

items.q: On a canoe trip, 2 children sit in each canoe. There are 4 canoes. How many children?
items.e: 4 groups of 2: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 children. (4 is the number of canoes.)

items.q: Olivia gives 3 maple cookies to each of 3 friends. How many cookies is that?
items.e: 3 groups of 3: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 cookies.
Make groups of 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. That is 5 pairs.

items.q: In gym class, there are 2 basketball teams. Each team has 5 players. How many players?
items.e: 2 groups of 5: 5 + 5 = 10 players.

items.q: At soccer, 6 children each get half an orange. How many whole oranges is that?
items.e: 2 halves make 1 orange. 6 halves make 3 pairs. That is 3 oranges.

items.q: Priya eats the 2 shaded pieces of this pizza. How much of the pizza is that?
items.e: 2 of 4 equal pieces are two fourths. Two fourths is the same as one half.
